h.strategy: Obvious hypotheses (an edit matters more when an alternative path is removed; strong components help more when connected) score zero even if true. Target effects that real measurements often show but intuition misses: ceiling effects (a normally helpful edit helps less, or hurts, when the parent is already strong); redundancy (two strong components in parallel are worth less than either alone suggests); substitution (a cheap or 'weak' option beats a strong one when capacity elsewhere is high); and sign reversals of an edit's usual effect under specific conditions. Each hypothesis needs a concrete mechanism. Vary the edited field and the conditioning field across hypotheses, and include both HIGHER and LOWER directions.

hyps.why: With edge 0 removed, node 1 carries no signal, so deleting edge 2 costs essentially nothing, whereas it normally removes a useful path.
With a skip-3 residual carrying the signal, a cheap pool on edge 0 costs less than it would otherwise (substitution).
A pool on the last hop is less damaging when a direct skip supplies the main feature path to the output.
A pool on the direct edge cannot act as an identity shortcut, so it adds little beside a weak conv path (it needs a skip).
Node 2 already receives strong conv features from edge 1, so the extra 1x1 mixing path is redundant.
With the skip-3 residual present, a weak 1x1 branch via node 2 contributes little, so the gain is smaller than when no shortcut exists.
Two parallel 1x1 convs into the output are redundant, so the second adds little.
A skip after a conv3x3 makes a clean one-conv path to the output, which beats the alternatives on edge 4.
A skip after a conv3x3 on edge 1 yields a shallow, easy-to-train feature path into the output.
A skip on edge 0 followed by a conv3x3 on edge 4 gives a shallow one-conv route, which is better than the alternatives on edge 0.
